memories.memory_text: I was told that Tuvia issues a direct order to Asael to send a message to Zus, who will then inform Viktor of approaching forces.

grounded_facts: An urgent communication event triggered by Aron's arrival and intelligence report to Tuvia, leading to a chain of command actions.
memories.memory_text: I saw Aron race into camp and whisper urgently to Tuvia, and then Tuvia called my name and ordered me to send a message to Zus so he could warn Viktor they were coming.

grounded_facts: Asael informs Tuvia that Lazar spotted another patrol approaching.
memories.memory_text: I told Tuvia that Lazar spotted another patrol and they're getting closer.

grounded_facts: Tuvia perceives a strange sound from the forest, prompting immediate attention and concern.
memories.memory_text: I heard Tuvia ask if I heard a strange sound from the forest, and it made me alert.

grounded_facts: Asael reports that the captured man is a German SS scout.
memories.memory_text: I told Tuvia that the man was a scout, stating what I knew so the group could act on it.

grounded_facts: Documents found on the scout reveal that a full division is assigned to surround the forest, with an assault planned in two days.
memories.memory_text: I found documents in the scout's pouch and saw that they reveal a full German division is assigned to surround the forest, with the assault beginning in two days on Passover.

grounded_facts: Bella names her murdered son before killing the German scout.
memories.memory_text: I remember Bella speaking about her son David Kagan, saying he was fifteen, had blue eyes, and played the piano, right before she struck the scout with a sharpened hoe.

grounded_facts: A spontaneous gathering in the clearing where the captured German scout is interrogated, tortured, and ultimately killed by the group.
memories.memory_text: I was there when the group gathered around the scout—kicking, punching, breaking a stick on his back, shouting 'Justice!'—until he was killed, and Tuvia chose not to stop it.

grounded_facts: A German SS scout is captured and brought to the clearing by the group, marking a critical intelligence and moral turning point.
memories.memory_text: I saw the group bring the captured German SS scout to the clearing, hands tied, and I witnessed the violence unfold—kicks, punches, the breaking of a stick across his back, Aron fleeing, the chorus of 'Justice!', and Tuvia closing his eyes as it ended.

grounded_facts: Tuvia witnesses the escalating torture and eventual killing of the German scout but does not stop it, marking a moral collapse.
memories.memory_text: I looked at Malbin and Shimon and saw how undone they were by what we had witnessed — the torture and killing of the German scout, and Tuvia just standing there, doing nothing.

grounded_facts: The group collectively kills the captured German scout in a ritualized act of vengeance, crossing a moral threshold.
memories.memory_text: I saw the group attack the captured German scout—kicking him, breaking a stick across his back—and heard them shout 'Justice!' over and over until he was dead, and afterward, I noticed how we all stood there, staring at what we'd done and beginning to understand what we had become.

grounded_facts: Zus, Tuvia, Viktor, and bodyguards gather in a clearing before departing into the woods for an operation.
memories.memory_text: I joined Zus and the bodyguards in the clearing where Tuvia and Viktor were about to head into the woods.

grounded_facts: Zus comments that Asael doesn't look good, mirroring Asael's own remark.
memories.memory_text: I heard Zus say I didn't look good, so I told him I could say the same about him and asked where he got his jacket.

grounded_facts: Zus implies he took the Nazi jacket from a dead former owner.
memories.memory_text: I was there when Zus told me about the Nazi jacket, saying the former owner no longer had need of it, and then he winked at me.

grounded_facts: Zus secretly hands a revolver to Asael during an embrace, instructing him to hide it.
memories.memory_text: I felt Zus shove a revolver into my pocket during our embrace and whispered for me to hide it.

grounded_facts: Zus informs Asael that Wolnicky stores ammunition in his barn with no guard.
memories.memory_text: I was told by Zus that Wolnicky stores ammunition in his barn with no guard.

grounded_facts: Zus asks Asael to embrace him, then slaps him fondly on the cheek after passing the revolver.
memories.memory_text: I remember Zus asking me to embrace him, and after passing the revolver, he slapped me fondly on the cheek.

grounded_facts: Viktor hands Tuvia a German wanted poster with a bounty, commenting on its unflattering nature.
Viktor shows Tuvia a wanted poster offering fifty thousand marks for his capture, mocking its depiction.
memories.memory_text: I was told the Germans are offering fifty thousand marks for Tuvia's capture, and that the poster's likeness isn't flattering—too Jewish, they said.

grounded_facts: Asael advises Tuvia not to show the wanted poster around, noting that some would betray him for less than the bounty.
memories.memory_text: I advised Tuvia not to show the wanted poster around, because I know some would betray him for less than that bounty.

grounded_facts: Asael encourages an elder, addressing him as 'tateh', to start moving for evacuation.
memories.memory_text: I called out to the elder, urging him to come with me as we started to evacuate.

grounded_facts: Oppenheim resists evacuation momentarily, worried about leaving his tools behind.
memories.memory_text: I saw Oppenheim hesitate, worried about leaving his tools behind.

grounded_facts: Riva assigns each elderly person a child to accompany them, likely to assist in evacuation.
memories.memory_text: I noticed Riva assigning each elderly person a child to help them during the evacuation.

grounded_facts: The Bielski camp begins urgent preparations to evacuate due to approaching danger.
memories.memory_text: I was part of the urgent preparations when the camp began evacuating due to the approaching danger.

grounded_facts: An aerial attack by German Stuka dive bombers on the Bielski camp forces immediate evacuation and defensive actions.
memories.memory_text: I witnessed the aerial attack by German Stuka dive bombers that forced us to evacuate immediately.

grounded_facts: Tamara secures her newborn under her coat, likely to protect the infant from danger.
memories.memory_text: I saw Tamara tuck her newborn under her coat to keep the baby safe.

grounded_facts: Asael yells at Malbin to evacuate people from the bunkers.
memories.memory_text: I yelled at Malbin to get the people out of the bunkers when I saw him panicking in the smoke.

grounded_facts: Asael uses pantomime and speech to convey the need to hold off the enemy and assigns positions.
Asael communicates the plan to hold off Germans, assigning team members to positions.
memories.memory_text: I used pantomime and shouted to make sure they understood—'HOLD...THEM...OFF!'—then pointed out where each of us needed to be, assigning positions with Levine, Miriam, Lazar, Rosa, Schmuel, and me taking cover to hold the line.

grounded_facts: After regaining his footing, Tuvia realizes the bombing has ceased.
memories.memory_text: I saw Tuvia regain his footing and suddenly realize the bombing had stopped.

grounded_facts: Malbin overcomes fear and rushes through danger to reach injured Tuvia.
Malbin repeatedly asks Tuvia if he is alright, showing concern.
Tuvia communicates that the Germans are coming, conveying urgent threat.
A sudden German assault involving bombing and imminent threat forces the group into emergency action.
memories.memory_text: I saw Malbin overcome his fear and race through the danger to reach Tuvia, who was lying in the open, and I heard him repeatedly ask if Tuvia was alright; then Tuvia managed to warn us that the Germans were coming, just as explosions erupted around us.

grounded_facts: Tuvia physically grabs Asael's shoulders to emphasize urgency before giving orders.
memories.memory_text: I felt Tuvia grab my shoulders, his hands firm, pulling me close to make sure I was listening.

grounded_facts: Tuvia instructs Asael not to engage in direct combat but to delay the enemy and retreat.
memories.memory_text: I was told not to fight, just to slow them down and then join the others.

grounded_facts: Tuvia and Asael share a wordless, fierce embrace after the command is given.
memories.memory_text: After I nodded, I shared a fierce, wordless embrace with Tuvia—we didn’t need to say anything more.

grounded_facts: Asael entrusts Chaya to Tuvia, ensuring her evacuation despite her resistance.
memories.memory_text: I pushed Chaya toward Tuvia and told him to take her, knowing she'd be safer with him as we retreated.

grounded_facts: Chaya resists separation by clinging to Asael's arm.
memories.memory_text: I felt Chaya cling to my arm, resisting when I tried to send her away.

grounded_facts: Tuvia compels Chaya to leave with him despite her resistance.
memories.memory_text: I saw Tuvia tell Chaya to come and then force her to leave with him despite her hesitation.

grounded_facts: Lazar is killed instantly by a grenade thrown from the woods.
memories.memory_text: I saw Lazar running from tree to tree, firing steadily, when a grenade flew out of the woods and landed at his feet, killing him instantly.

grounded_facts: Miriam shouts 'GO!' to prompt the others to flee while she covers them.
memories.memory_text: I heard Miriam shout 'GO!' at me and the others, and I knew it was time to run.

grounded_facts: Miriam suppresses attackers to cover retreat, then is hit but continues firing.
memories.memory_text: I saw Miriam keep the attackers pinned down so Sara and I could move, and then she got hit but kept firing, her finger locked on the trigger even as she was going down.

grounded_facts: An ambush by Assault Troops at the camp results in casualties and forces a retreat.
memories.memory_text: I had no choice but to break off and retreat into the woods when more enemy troops began firing at us from the flank.

grounded_facts: Asael and the others retreat into the woods after being outflanked.
memories.memory_text: I had no choice but to retreat into the woods with the others after we were outflanked and more enemy troops opened fire.

Tuvia tells Lilka to use her revolver on herself before being taken by the Germans, a grim directive reflecting the stakes of capture.
memories.memory_text: I saw Lilka silently offer her revolver to Tuvia, and I watched him check the clip before telling her to use it on herself if the Germans were to take her. She nodded, and I knew then that they were preparing for death rather than capture.

grounded_facts: Tuvia sinks to his knees, unable to speak or make decisions, signaling a collapse of leadership under the pressure of Asael's absence and the group's dire situation.
memories.memory_text: I saw Tuvia sink to his knees, unable to speak or make a decision, staring at the swamp like it was the end of everything.

grounded_facts: A group of fugitives reaches the edge of the Krasnaya Gorka Swamp, facing a critical decision on whether to enter, under threat of imminent German arrival and aerial detection.
memories.memory_text: I was there when the group reached the edge of the Krasnaya Gorka Swamp, and I heard the warning—they're coming—so I knew we had to act fast.

grounded_facts: Asael confronts Tuvia for halting the group, demanding action and reasserting the need to move forward.
memories.memory_text: I confronted Tuvia directly, asking 'Why aren't we moving?' because I needed him to act and not let the group stall under threat.

grounded_facts: Asael reappears, declares the enemy is coming, and demands the group move forward, restoring urgency and direction.
memories.memory_text: I returned and saw everyone turn to me; I handed a wounded comrade to Riva, shouted 'They're coming!' and insisted, 'We must keep going!' to get us moving again.

grounded_facts: Asael initiates the creation of a human chain using belts and linked arms to cross the swamp, which Tuvia endorses, restoring group cohesion and action.
Asael delivers a speech rejecting miracles and calling for collective strength, shifting the group's mindset from despair to action.
memories.memory_text: I stood up and told the group that nothing is impossible — we've already done the impossible. I made it clear that God won't part these waters; we will cross by our own strength. Then I took action, asking for belts and telling everyone to link arms, forming a human chain. I saw them respond, one by one offering their belts, and with Tuvia's endorsement, we moved as one.

grounded_facts: After reaching safety, the group experiences a wave of relief, culminating in contagious laughter.
The group arrives on the opposite bank after a dangerous crossing, marking a moment of survival and emotional release.
memories.memory_text: I felt the relief wash over us as we made it to the other side, pulling people up onto dry ground, and then someone laughed—it was sudden, unexpected—and soon we were all caught in the same wave of laughter, trembling with the release.

grounded_facts: The German tank fires at the riverbank, with the second round hitting and killing two brigade members.
memories.memory_text: I witnessed the tank fire at us, and the second round struck the riverbank, killing two of our brigade members.

grounded_facts: Asael, Lilka, Chaya, and other women provide covering fire to掩护 Tuvia and Malbin as they move.
memories.memory_text: I provided covering fire alongside Lilka, Chaya, and the other women to protect Tuvia and Malbin as they moved.

grounded_facts: Tuvia prepares grenades, throws satchel over Malbin, grabs his arm, and leads him under fire toward a tactical position.
memories.memory_text: I saw Tuvia grab grenades, throw the satchel over Malbin, grab his arm, and lead him under fire toward a flanking position.

grounded_facts: A coordinated German military advance using a tank and infantry to attack partisan forces near a riverbank and forest.
memories.memory_text: I saw the Germans launch a full attack with a tank and infantry moving toward our position near the riverbank and forest.

grounded_facts: Tuvia instructs the group to take only weapons and ammunition and to spread the word, establishing a new priority for evacuation.
memories.memory_text: I heard Tuvia tell me directly to take only weapons and ammunition and to spread the word, so I knew that was our top priority now.

grounded_facts: Tuvia gives Asael a German machine gun, symbolizing trust and operational readiness.
memories.memory_text: I was the first to reach Tuvia, and he handed me the German machine gun, which made me feel he trusted me with a key role in the evacuation.

grounded_facts: Tuvia directs Lilka to help move the injured into the forest, starting the evacuation process.
memories.memory_text: I saw Tuvia tell Lilka to help move the injured into the forest, and I realized the evacuation was starting right away.

grounded_facts: Tuvia throws a weapon to Shulman and sarcastically congratulates him on promotion, lightening the mood.
memories.memory_text: I saw Tuvia throw a weapon to Shulman and say sarcastically, 'You've been promoted. Congratulations!'—it lightened the mood after the battle.

grounded_facts: The two groups meet at the site of a destroyed tank to regroup, exchange information, and organize evacuation after a battle.
memories.memory_text: I remember the two groups meeting at the destroyed tank to regroup, exchange information, and organize the evacuation after the battle.

grounded_facts: Zus gives Bella the machine gun removed from the tank, arming her and showing trust.
memories.memory_text: I saw Zus hand Bella the machine gun from the tank, arming her before he moved forward.

grounded_facts: Tuvia declares the need to build a new camp, shifting the group's goal from survival to reorganization.
memories.memory_text: I heard Tuvia declare, 'We've got to build a new camp,' shifting our focus from mere survival to rebuilding.

grounded_facts: After confirming he will not return to his unit, Zus asks to join Tuvia's group, who accepts by embracing him.
memories.memory_text: I witnessed Zus refuse to return to his unit and ask Tuvia, 'Perhaps you have room for one more?' before they embraced fiercely.

grounded_facts: After a tense exchange, Tuvia and Zus embrace fiercely, resolving unspoken tensions and reaffirming loyalty.
memories.memory_text: I saw Tuvia and Zus lock into a fierce embrace after their tense exchange, and in that moment, I knew their bond was restored.

memories.memory_text: I appeared beside Tuvia, bringing a new problem and re-introducing concern, ending his moment of peace.

memories.memory_text: I watched the people being herded away and asked where they were taking them, but Zus hushed me—told me to just shut up, please.
I saw Papa’s torso behind the trough, just lying there… I couldn’t move, couldn’t speak—only whisper his name into the silence.
I said his name—'Aron'—when I saw him come up from the cellar, but he flinched away, wouldn't let us touch him, wouldn't say a word.
I couldn't stop shaking—I was drowning in it, the grief and panic pulling me under, and I couldn't breathe, couldn't think.
I heard a footstep in the dark and then saw him—Tuvia. I jumped up and ran to him, holding on as if I’d drown if I let go.
I told him—my voice shaking—'Papa and Mama. They killed them.' I couldn’t let go, not even after I said it.
I stood outside the farmhouse, heart pounding, scanning the trees and road for any movement while Zus was inside—every second felt like a breath held too long.
I can't believe Papa's dead. The words came out before I could stop them, right after we laughed like we used to—like nothing had changed.
Koscik has a pistol. I remembered that suddenly—how he once showed it to me—and I said it out loud, like it might be the first real thing we could do instead of just running.
I tried to keep the fire going, but the kindling was wet and wouldn't catch—then Shimon tore pages from a Hebrew book and lit them, and the flames finally rose.

Tuvia called my name sharply—'Asael!'—and told me to find food for the new people, his voice leaving no room for hesitation, so I moved toward the stores, already calculating how thin we could stretch the soup.
I brushed Aron's hair while the others gathered around the food, trying to keep some sense of care in the midst of all this loss.
I asked what an 'otriad' meant, and when Tuvia said it was an armed brigade, I said it right then—'Then we are the Bielski Otriad.'
I lay beside Tuvia in the ditch, cold earth under me, watching him loop the wire around the post—one end already set, taut across the road, waiting.
I saw the German soldier spot us and turn to run—I didn’t think, I just moved with Peretz, feet pounding the road, Jacov behind us with the rifle ready.
I remember closing in on the soldier, the crunch of gravel under my boots as Peretz and I brought him down, kicking until Jacov reached us and fired the final shot.
I didn't know where to go—I just ran, crashing into the wheat field, but it was the wrong side of the road. The spotlight hit me, and I saw soldiers pouring out, coming straight for me.
I realized too late that I'd gone too far—I had to double back toward the woods, but the soldiers were already moving to cut me off.
I dove to my knees and crawled as fast as I could, digging into the mud of the ditch with my hands, feeling it tear under my nails while voices closed in around me.
I stepped out of the dark cellar into the blinding light, and suddenly Zus was hugging me so tight I couldn’t breathe—I barely had time to register the sun before his arms crushed me.

I reached back into the cellar and brought Bella and Chaya out, their dresses dirty but fine, and when I showed the rifles and ammunition, I saw the way the others looked at me—not just as a survivor, but as someone who brought hope.
I grabbed Chaya's hand and shouted 'Don't panic. THIS WAY! GO!' as gunfire broke out, pulling her and the others toward the tree line while Tuvia yelled at me to keep moving.
I put my arm around Chaya as she started to cry—her body shaking against me—and then she looked up, her eyes searching mine like she was trying to find some promise there.
She held my gaze and asked if I would help her parents, then said if I rescued them, she would do anything for me—I froze, my voice caught, and I stammered out a confused yes.

I remember how exposed I felt stepping beyond the tree line—just open ground between us and the city, no cover, nothing. The air was colder out there, and I could see Novogrudok rising in the distance like a warning.
Zus pulled me into an embrace and whispered 'Hide this' as he shoved a revolver into my pocket—my hands trembled as I realized I was being trusted with something dangerous, something secret.
I shouted at Malbin to get them out of the bunkers — he hesitated, then ran. I couldn’t tell if he understood, but he moved.
Tuvia couldn’t hear, so I mimed firing a rifle and pointed to positions — he nodded, but I wasn’t sure if he truly understood until he finally agreed.
Tuvia grabbed my shoulders and told me not to fight—just to slow them down and then join the group. I nodded because I understood: this was the last order I might ever follow.
I pushed Chaya toward Tuvia and told her to go—she clung to my arm for a second, but I made her leave. I don’t know if I’ll see her again.

memories.memory_text: I shook my head when Rifka suggested I take false papers and stay in the city — I couldn't betray who I was, not while my family was out there.
I heard the footstep, then Asael leapt into my arms like I was the only thing keeping him alive — I held both him and Aron, silent, feeling the weight of what I had to carry now.
Zus appeared with a hatchet, looked at me like he wasn’t sure who I was anymore, then tossed me the mezuzah — that one gesture, 'Welcome home,' felt like both a test and a passing of responsibility.
I remember standing in the barn, Koscik pressing me to take in the laborers, and I could only ask—what am I supposed to do with them? How do I feed more when I can't even care for my own?
I stood in the doorway, rain soaking through my clothes, and asked the police captain if he knew who I was—he said nothing, but his wife’s face told me she understood the reckoning had come.

After I shot the first son lunging at me, the mother screamed and the captain tried to rise—I backed away and fired again, then turned the gun on the second son; it was over in seconds, but their faces are still with me.
I told Zus they are family — I had to say it firmly, even as he pulled me aside, because if we don’t hold that line, we lose what makes us more than just survivors.
I called for Asael to find food — not just for one, but for all of them — and I meant it, even if it means thinner soup for everyone.
I told Zus we can't become like them, that taking lives won't bring his family back, and for a moment I saw the same ghosts in his eyes that I carry.
When he named Asael, Peretz, and Jacov as his men, I felt the ground shift—then I asked him, 'You are making the decisions now?' and the silence after hung like a blade.
I tackled the Lieutenant as he reached for his pistol, and we rolled across the road fighting—clawing, punching, biting—until I slammed his head against the pavement.
The gunfire could be heard for miles—I said it out loud, my voice tight with worry, because the sound might bring more of them down on us.
I took the Schmeisser from Zus and checked it fast—chamber, grip, weight—making sure it was ready, because now there was no turning back.

Shimon stared at me, saying they thought I was bringing food, and kept pressing—did the farmers have guns, did they have dogs? I couldn’t answer. I just looked at him, while all around me, hungry faces watched, waiting for something I couldn’t give.

Zus was drunk, shouting at Lazar, slapping him over and over—I had to pull him off. When he lunged again, I yanked him back hard, sent him falling. I told him no mistakes, then reminded him of what would happen to Asael if we weren’t careful.
I saw Asael emerge from the root cellar, blinking in the light, and I said, 'Thank God.'
I turned to Koscik's wife and said, 'Thank you,' before she turned away and told us to go.
I told Asael to go talk to Chaya after I caught him staring at her—she turned when I called her name, and he blushed like a boy.
I told Asael to go with Zus to the Piznarksi granary to make sure he understood my orders.

I remember sitting there, the violin playing outside, and hearing Shimon offer to say Kaddish—but I barely heard him. I was thinking only of her: how she called me a failure, how we weren't really married, how I couldn't give her what she needed.
I told Zus I was going in with him, even though he ordered me to stay with the truck. He said he gave the orders tonight, but I couldn't stay behind.
I gave Zus our parents' mezuzah before he left the truck. I don't know if it was for his luck or mine, but he took it without a word and walked into the dark.
I felt the weight of Zus’s words like a blow when he said fighters die so the malbushim can live — the bitterness in his voice, the blood on the package, it all hit me at once.
I asked him to come back to us, and when I said 'You are my brother,' he only replied, 'So you remember,' without even looking at me.
I can't stop coughing, the fever won't break, and the bottle is empty again—but I can still hear them arguing outside, as if I'm not falling apart in here.
I told both Arkady and Asael their rations would be cut for a week—same punishment for both—even though Asael looked at me like I’d betrayed him, and the others were watching to see if I’d back down.
When Asael told me the rumors—that I drink too much and can’t lead—part of me wanted to deny it, but all I could say was 'Maybe they're right,' and then I walked away before he could see more.
I said it plainly, weak and burning with fever—'I am not a leader'—because I couldn't carry it anymore, not even in the dark of the bunker.

I told her I couldn't keep the living alive — that Tamara and the father were responsible — but then she said the words that stopped me: 'She was raped by the Nazis.' I closed my eyes. I was so tired of deciding who lived and who didn't.

After she kissed me — first softly, then deeper — I remember the smell of her washed hair, the warmth of her skin. I whispered her name, and when she said she wasn't afraid of me, something broke inside. I didn't stop the kiss.
I knelt beside Aron, holding him as he wept silently under the tree, and whispered to the Lord, begging for mercy after all we’ve done.
I heard Malbin’s voice from the edge of the forest—pale, shaken—and the words 'Viktor is here' cut through the silence, stopping my thoughts.
Viktor demanded I hand over command of my fighters, saying his orders gave him authority over all partisans—and that if I refused, I'd be labeled a deserter.
He handed me a German wanted poster with my face on it—fifty thousand marks for my capture—and said the likeness was too Jewish, as if it were a joke.
I grabbed people and dragged them into cover as the cannon fire tore up the ground—I had to move fast before more were hit.
I grabbed Asael by the shoulders and told him not to fight, just slow them down and fall back — we couldn’t afford a stand, only survival.
Chaya resisted when I tried to take her — she was clinging to Asael — but I forced her to come with me, pulling her away to keep moving.
I dropped to my knees, staring at the swamp—Asael wasn't coming back, and I had no answer, no order to give. The weight of all their eyes on me, but I couldn't speak.
Lilka knelt beside me and took my hand—her touch pulled me back, even as the plane appeared above. I felt the moment shift, something reigniting beneath the numbness.

I couldn't help it—we were all laughing, lying there on the ground, soaked and shaking, but finally safe. The sound spread through us like fire, and for a moment, none of the weight was on my shoulders.
I knelt beside Shimon as he whispered that I was sent by God to save them. I called it ridiculous, but when he thanked me—and Him—I couldn't hold back the tears.

memories.memory_text: I stepped toward the farmer with the pitchfork, ready to make him give us food, but Asael held me back—I had to say it, that we’d be back, so he’d know this wasn’t over.
I heard a noise from the cupboard and grabbed the hatchet—someone could be inside, could be a threat, and I won’t let anything happen to us.
When the boy came up from the root cellar—Aron—I moved to embrace him, but he flinched back, silent and scared, and I had to stop myself from reaching further.
I grabbed Asael, shouting at him to stop—his crying, his shaking—it was too much, and I didn’t know what else to do.
I saw the mezuzah in my hand, then tossed it to Tuvia—no words needed. He caught it, and that was that.
I raised my rifle and thought about crushing that man's head — he's lucky I didn't, after all the shit I've eaten from his kind.
When Tuvia questioned me, I told him plainly — no, not all, but some I will kill, because this ends now.
I laughed when Tuvia smacked me and mocked me like Papa used to—right after I farted. Even with Papa gone, that old stupid joke still hit.
I told Tuvia we can't feed these people, and then made sure he remembered to ask Koscik for the pistol—after he asked for food.
I sent Tuvia to get food, and instead he brought back more hungry mouths—no supplies, just another burden. When I asked if he got the gun, he showed me only four bullets.
I took the pistol from Tuvia’s belt and checked the cylinder—only one bullet left. I asked him how it felt to kill them, and he told me to shut up.
I looked at the huddled people—women, children, the old teacher—and said they’d slow us down. Tuvia joked, but I meant it: we can’t move fast with them.
I loaded Wilencki's gun while Tuvia kept talking about not making enemies, but all I could think was blood for blood — his mercy won't bring back Mama or Papa.
I asked Asael to come with us — Peretz, Jacov, and me — and when Tuvia challenged me, I looked him in the eye and made him ask, 'You are making the decisions now?'
Peretz and I were backing out of that house, shooting into the dark as screams rose behind us — I could feel the kick of my rifle, the heat of it, and the weight of what we’d just done.
I shouted into the night — 'We are the Bielski Otriad! We are Jews!' — faces watched from windows, silent, and I made them see us, made them know we weren’t running anymore.
I wrapped the wire tight around the tree with Peretz and Jacov, making sure it was secure for the ambush.
I found a beautiful knife in the saddlebags after we took the motorcyclist down—lifted it up like a trophy, felt the weight of it in my hand.
I smashed the Sergeant's nose with the knife handle and ripped the Schmeisser from him, firing point-blank—his coat caught fire as he went down.
I swung the Schmeisser toward the staff car and opened fire, shattering the windows and dropping the officer and the woman inside—Tuvia was clear, alive.
I was high from the kill, blood all over me, and I didn't care about the noise—Tuvia could say whatever he wanted, but that man pissed on my head and now he's dead.
I handed Tuvia the Schmeisser like a prize—he took it without a word, and I kept moving, telling Peretz and Jacov to search the car and me to check the body for ammo.
I ran back under fire to grab Peretz’s rifle after we got him into the trees—he bled in my hands and I wasn’t leaving his weapon for the enemy.
Tuvia ripped my rifle out of my hands—just as I was about to act—and shot the spotlight, throwing everything into blackness.
I was crouched in the woods with Tuvia and Ben Zion, waiting in silence until Tuvia said 'Now'—then we moved out, weapons up, closing in on the farm.
I called out to Koscik, told him to stop fooling with the sheep and pull up his pants—then I saw him hanging from the threshing hook, that sign swinging from his chest like some sick joke.
I pulled Asael into a mighty embrace — my brother, alive and standing in the light after all this time. I couldn’t speak, just held him tight until he joked I was crushing him.
When Bella stepped out behind Asael, I looked her over — dirty dress, but it was clear she was something special. I said, 'Asael... Well, well..' and meant every bit of it.

I was still breathing hard from being with Bella in the woods—her skin warm against mine—when I heard the screaming. I didn’t have time to think, just grabbed my rifle and snapped, 'QUIET! NOT ANOTHER WORD!!!' like a command from my bones.
The gunfire cracked through the camp, and I saw two bodies drop—no time to process, only to act. I barked the order to silence everyone, knowing one more sound could bring the police straight to us.
I shouted into the trees, 'Next one is to the head!' after Kessely got hit — they needed to know we weren’t playing, that we’d kill to protect our own.
After they ran, I told Tuvia his diplomacy was shit — we should’ve killed the milkman, and now we’ve got two dead and no shelter with winter coming.
I pulled the blood-soaked package from my coat and said, 'Medicine.' That was all he needed to know.
He said 'Come back to us,' and then 'You are my brother.' I answered only, 'So you remember.' I didn't look at him.

I stood there while Gramov sneered and said he beat Lova because he was a Jew—then laughed like it was nothing. When Panchenko made him say 'I apologize, Jew,' I felt the weight of the glass in my hand, knowing swallowing that vodka meant accepting the insult, but refusing it would mean chaos.

I stood there with my rifle in hand, knowing what Viktor would say before he even said it — that my brothers were just another sacrifice for the cause, and that my loyalty to them meant nothing to him.
